INSIDE THE PROCESS / 004

How we think
about an edge.

Inspired by published work and interviews with successful bettors—not a copy of anyone’s private model.

Read Benter’s original paper ↗
01

Start with the market

Compare the moneyline to a no-vig baseline. Bill Benter’s published racing work combined his model with market information; that idea doesn’t automatically transfer to basketball or football.

02

Look for what changed

Track injuries and line movement, an approach described by Gadoon “Spanky” Kyrollos. Avoid counting news twice when a model or price already includes it.

03

Test probabilities, not stories

Use time-ordered backtests, calibration, Brier score and log loss against a market-only baseline. Closing-line value is a diagnostic—not proof of profit.

04

Keep referee effects experimental

Assign no adjustment until tested out of sample after accounting for team strength, venue, rest and market price.

THE ML LAB
INTERACTIVE TOOL

Moneyline calculator

⌁

BREAK-EVEN—Minimum win rate
NO-VIG BASELINE—Proportional estimate
WIN PROFIT—Original stake returned too
EXPECTED VALUE—Only if assumption is right

Expected value is a long-run mathematical average, not a likely single-game outcome. Losing the stake is possible. NFL ties and special settlement rules can change this simple two-outcome illustration.

MODEL STATUS
RESEARCH STAGE

Transparent by design.

There is no trained Line Lab model or verified betting edge yet. Current estimates are attributed to public sources. Referee and schedule notes aren’t added to those forecasts.

01

Build a timestamped history of prices, lineups, rest, crews and outcomes.

02

Train with past information only; compare against the market on later seasons.

03

Publish calibration, errors and results before claiming a predictive advantage.
